g. Executive responsibilities

The implementation of this Focus Group Discussion (FGD) involves three main roles, namely the main facilitator, notes or minutes takers, and field coordinator. Each role has complementary functions and responsibilities to ensure that the data collection process runs effectively, participatory, and produces accurate information.
Main facilitator

The lead facilitator oversees the entire FGD process, ensuring the discussion is neutral, inclusive, well-managed, and aligned with the assessment objectives. Before the FGD, the facilitator understands the climate vulnerability and resilience framework, prepares guiding questions and participatory methods, and coordinates with the field coordinator about participant profiles. During the FGD, the facilitator explains objectives and rules, ensures participant consent, guides discussion with open and probing questions, manages group dynamics, maintains focus on climate vulnerability and adaptation issues, and ensures equal participation. After the session, the facilitator summarises key points for clarity and works with the minutes and field coordinator to review findings and identify follow-up actions.
Note takers

The minutes are responsible for systematically and accurately documenting the entire FGD process and its results, ensuring the integrity of qualitative data. Before the session, the minutes prepare recording formats, participant information, and necessary documentation tools. During the FGD, they record key discussion points, examples, differing views, quotes, and visual outputs, without actively participating unless clarification is needed. Afterwards, the minutes compiles a clear and organised report, categorising findings on vulnerability, risk, adaptive capacity, and resilience strategies, while maintaining data security and confidentiality.
Field coordinator

The field coordinator oversees coordination, logistics, and technical arrangements for the FGD, serving as a liaison between the team and the fishing community. Before the session, the coordinator works with local leaders to set a suitable time and venue, ensures participants meet the criteria, and prepares all logistical and administrative needs. During the FGD, the coordinator manages attendance, handles technical issues, and ensures participant comfort and safety. Afterwards, they express appreciation to the community, archive documentation, and report the activity to the programme team.
h. Procedure for implementation of FGD
The duration of the meeting and the group number.

According to Barbour (2018), Denzin and Lincoln (2018), Flick (2018), and Krueger and Casey (2015), the recommended duration for a Focus Group Discussion (FGD) is usually 60-90 minutes, especially when discussing complex or sensitive topics. Discussions should not exceed two hours, as longer sessions can lead to participant fatigue and decreased data quality.

In terms of group size, the recommended number of participants is generally 6-12 individuals. Groups of this size are considered optimal for facilitating meaningful interactions, ensuring diversity of perspectives, and maintaining effective moderation. Smaller groups (6-8 participants) are often preferred for in-depth or sensitive discussions, while slightly larger groups (8-12 participants) may be appropriate for broader exploratory topics.
Participant identification and selection stage

The participant identification stage is a very important first step in the implementation of the Focus Group Discussion (FGD) for the assessment of the vulnerability and climate resilience of tuna fishing communities. This process aims to ensure that the participants involved are truly representative of the target group and have relevant experience and knowledge on the topic of climate change and its impact on socio-economic life.

The number of participants in each FGD is set between six to twelve people per group. This number is considered ideal to keep the dynamics of the discussion interactive, allow the active participation of all participants, and remain under control in the facilitation process. Groups that are too large have the potential to reduce speaking opportunities for some participants, while groups that are too small can limit the diversity of perspectives.

Participant identification is carried out based on criteria that have been determined for each target group. This process is carried out through coordination with the village government, the head of fishermen's groups, community leaders, or other parties who understand the social structure of the community. The selection of participants must consider the diversity of ages, experiences, and economic backgrounds in order to obtain a representative picture.

For tuna fishermen groups, the selected participants must be active fishermen who have been catching tuna for at least three years. This criterion is important so that participants have sufficient experience in observing changes in seasonal patterns, weather conditions, and the dynamics of catches over time. In addition, the selected fishermen are prioritised who have directly faced changes in weather conditions or uncertain sea situations, so that discussions can produce information based on real experiences.

For the group of women in tuna fishery households, participants are fishermen's wives or women who are part of fishermen's households. They must be actively involved in managing the household economy, such as managing finances, managing the proceeds of fish sales, or running an ancillary business. This engagement is important so that the discussion can illustrate the impact of climate change on family economic stability and household well-being.

For the migrant worker group, participants are individuals who work in the tuna fisheries sector outside their home area, either as crew members, processing workers, and other support sectors. They were chosen because they have different perspectives on job uncertainty, labour mobility, and economic risks that may be affected by climate change and the dynamics of the fishing industry.

For community leader groups, participants consist of village heads, traditional leaders, fishermen's group leaders, or other community leaders who have a role in decision-making or social influence in the community. Their presence is important to provide institutional perspectives, local policies, as well as collective strategies that have been or can be implemented to improve community resilience to climate change.

The entire participant identification process must be carried out in a transparent, inclusive, and non-discriminatory manner. The implementation team is obliged to ensure that the selected participants are willing to participate voluntarily and understand the purpose of the activity. With the right selection process, the FGD is expected to be able to produce credible, representative, and relevant information for vulnerability analysis and community-based adaptation planning.
i. Logistics preparation

Logistical preparation is an important stage that must be carried out before the implementation of the Focus Group Discussion (FGD) to ensure that the activity runs effectively, systematically, and is well documented. All equipment must be ensured to be available, functioning properly, and in accordance with the needs of the facilitation method to be used.

The FGD team must prepare a question guide based on the objectives of assessing climate vulnerability and resilience in the tuna fishing community. This guide helps the Facilitator keep the discussion focused, in-depth, and relevant, and should be reviewed to ensure clear language and suitability to the local context. The team must also provide participants with an informed consent form before the session, explaining the purpose, benefits, process, data use, and confidentiality. The Facilitator ensures participants understand the information and give voluntary consent before the FGD begins.

The team must prepare adequate notebooks and stationery to support documentation, allowing minutes and participants to record key points and reflections. With participant consent, a recorder may be used to ensure accurate documentation, and recordings must be securely stored for analysis purposes only. Flipcharts should also be provided as visual aids to capture key points, diagrams, and participatory outputs such as vulnerability matrices or seasonal maps. All logistical equipment must be checked beforehand to ensure completeness and proper functioning for a smooth FGD implementation.
j. Facilitation guide per target group discussion
Opening stage (±10 minutes)

The opening stage of the FGD is crucial for building trust, participation, and a conducive discussion environment. The facilitator introduces the team and clarifies their roles, explains the purpose of the FGD in simple and relevant terms, and emphasizes that the discussion is to understand participants’ experiences, not to evaluate them. Participants are assured that there are no right or wrong answers, and that all opinions are valued. The facilitator also explains confidentiality, seeks consent (including for recording if used), and ensures voluntary participation. The session concludes with brief participant introductions to create a comfortable and open atmosphere before starting the main discussion.
Core discussion (±60 minutes)

Core discussions are the main part of the FGD which aims to dig up in-depth information on climate change exposure, sensitivity, and adaptation capacity. The facilitator guides the discussion using open-ended questions that have been compiled in the facilitation guide.

The implementation of Focus Group Discussion (FGD) in assessing the vulnerability and climate resilience of the tuna fishing community was carried out separately based on the target group. This separation aims to ensure that each group can openly convey their experiences, perceptions, and adaptation strategies in accordance with their respective social roles and positions. The facilitation approach must be participatory, inclusive, gender-sensitive, and respectful of local social and cultural norms.
FGD tuna fishers

The FGD with tuna fishermen aims to directly understand the impact of climate change on fishing activities, production stability, safety risks, and adaptation capacity owned by fishermen. The discussion focused on the real experiences of fishermen in dealing with changes in marine environmental conditions.

The facilitator began by exploring fishermen's perceptions of the changes that have occurred in recent years, especially related to the fishing season, wind patterns, waves, currents, and the level of difficulty in predicting the weather. The discussion was directed to identify whether there was a shift in tuna location, a change in catch depth, or an increase in distance to sea. Facilitators need to encourage participants to provide concrete examples based on personal experiences.

Furthermore, the discussion explored the level of sensitivity of fishermen to these changes. Facilitators explore how seasonal and weather changes impact catches, operational costs, frequency of sea trips, and household income. Occupational safety aspects also need to be discussed, including the increased risk of accidents due to extreme weather.

In the adaptation capacity section, the facilitator explored strategies that fishermen have carried out to adjust, such as changes in sea schedules, the use of weather information technology, diversification of fishing gear, or changes in species targets. Discussions also included fishers' access to climate information, group support, and government assistance.

In facilitating discussions, facilitators must ensure that all participants have the opportunity to speak, that there is no domination of certain individuals, and that the discussion remains focused on aspects of climate change and not just the issue of market prices or trade policies.
FGD women in tuna fisheries households

The FGD with women in tuna fisheries households aims to understand the impact of climate change on family welfare, household economic stability, and survival strategies carried out by women. This discussion is important because women are often the managers of household finances and the ones in charge of meeting the basic needs of the family.
The facilitator must create a comfortable and safe atmosphere for participants to speak openly. The approach used should be less formal and provide room for reflection on everyday experiences.

The discussion began by exploring changes in family income that were felt due to fluctuations in catches. The facilitator then explored its impact on meeting food needs, children's education, health, and changes in food consumption patterns. Additional workload aspects, both in the form of side hustles and increased domestic responsibilities, also need to be discussed.

In the adaptation capacity section, facilitators explore strategies that women carry out to overcome economic difficulties, such as rearranging spending, finding additional businesses, utilising social networks, or joining savings and loan groups. Discussions must be maintained so as not to cause a sense of blame for certain parties and remain focused on the experiences and solutions developed.
FGD migrant workers

The FGD with migrant workers aimed to understand the level of vulnerability of this group to climate change that impacts the fisheries sector and related employment. Migrant workers are often in economically and socially vulnerable positions, so the facilitation approach must be empathetic and guarantee the confidentiality of information.

The discussion was directed at exploring whether climate change affects job stability, contract duration, or job opportunities in the fisheries sector. Facilitators need to identify the impact on income stability and the risk of job loss due to declining productivity in the fisheries sector.

In the adaptation capacity section, facilitators explore strategies that migrant workers use to deal with uncertainty, such as finding employment alternatives, improving skills, or utilising social networks. Facilitators are obliged to keep the discussion atmosphere safe and not force participants to disclose information that is sensitive or potentially harmful to them.
FGD community leaders

The FGD with community leaders aims to obtain a comprehensive picture of the vulnerability and adaptation capacity of communities at the institutional and local governance levels. Discussions are more strategic and reflective, with a focus on the dynamics of the community as a whole.

Facilitators explore observed environmental changes at the village or community level, including impacts on key economic sectors, especially tuna fisheries. The discussion was directed at identifying the groups most vulnerable to climate change, such as small-scale fishers, women heads of households, or poor households.

In terms of adaptation capacity, the facilitator explored the efforts that have been made by the community, both through customary mechanisms, village policies, and government programme support. The discussion also included institutional readiness to deal with long-term climate risks as well as the need for additional support.

Facilitators must keep the discussion constructive and not turn into a political forum or a place to blame each other. The main focus is collective learning and identification of opportunities to strengthen community resilience.

The entire facilitation process per target group must be carried out by upholding the principles of participatory, inclusive, neutral, and ethical. The results of the discussions from each group will be analysed in an integrated manner to identify the level of exposure, sensitivity, and adaptation capacity at the individual, household, and community levels, as the basis for the preparation of recommendations to strengthen the climate resilience of tuna fishing communities.
Closing stage of FGD (15 minutes)

The closing stage is an important part of the Focus Group Discussion (FGD)  process because it ensures that all the results of the discussion have been properly understood, validated by the participants, and closed ethically and professionally. At this stage, the facilitator plays a role in consolidating the results of the discussion and maintaining a positive atmosphere until the end of the activity.
